proposed_edges.relationship: Kennedy and John Lewis Gaddis jointly designed and taught Yale’s Studies in Grand Strategy course (2000), alongside Charles Hill and Paul Bracken.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Yale’s original announcement, 18 January 2000, body paragraphs 2–5, especially paragraph beginning “Kennedy and John Gaddis”: they joined Hill and Bracken “in designing the course” and “all four will teach”. Kennedy’s preceding statement stresses seeing the broader strategic picture; the following paragraph describes historical primary readings. Yale’s On Grand Strategy notice (6 April 2018), first body paragraph, confirms the sustained co-teaching and identifies Gaddis’s book as reflecting on it. This is a documented teaching collaboration, classified as an undirected contribution; neither co-authorship of Gaddis’s 2018 book nor agreement on every strategic interpretation is claimed. Course materials and the book remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The author-hosted synopsis of Ferguson’s The Cash Nexus (2001) challenges Kennedy’s economic explanation of international power by emphasizing political forces shaping economic development.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author’s own book page, synopsis paragraphs 2–3: “Paul Kennedy has claimed that economics provided the key to international power”; it counters with “political events and institutions have often dominated economic development”. This is a synopsis-level relationship, not a fresh reading of the book’s argument. The publisher’s Description independently states that war drives financial innovation and economic development. Original year 2001 is explicitly confirmed in Ferguson’s About page, paragraph beginning “The latter won”; the 21 February 2002 date on the book page is the trade paperback date, as identified on the publisher page. Both books remain unread; the claim does not attribute detailed arguments or pages to either. Kennedy’s existing military contribution already preserves his later concession about economic determinism; this adds a named incoming critic.

review.reason: Synopsis on Ferguson's own site names Kennedy as an exponent of the 'conventional wisdom' that economic change drives political change, then states 'political events and institutions have often dominated economic development'. proposed_edges.relationship: In the essay reprinted as Daring to Undeceive (original 2021; reprint 2022), Ferguson explicitly borrows Kennedy’s phrase “imperial overstretch” to interpret interwar Britain in a comparison with American power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ferguson, Daring to Undeceive, Hoover Digest, Winter 2022, printed p. 118 (PDF page 120), second body paragraph: “imperial overstretch,” “to borrow a phrase from Paul Kennedy”. The continuation on printed p. 119 puts Britain’s thinly spread imperial resources into the analogy with America. Printed p. 128 carries the permission line identifying the Economist original as copyright 2021; exact original day/title not independently established. Selected publisher PDF text read, including those passages and the closing attribution; screenshot requests failed with cache miss, so no page-image reading is claimed. The original publisher’s site was unavailable to search because of robots.txt. The edge concerns this explicitly credited concept alone and does not imply endorsement of Kennedy’s whole thesis or withdrawal of Ferguson’s earlier criticism.
